#| echo: false

An agent that discovers a law by experiment has two things a plain fit does
not: a language model that knows a lot of physics, and tools that let it
choose its own experiments. Is the combination better than simpler methods?
The honest answer depends on what "better" is measured against, and the
comparisons are easy to rig by accident.

This lesson sets the agent of the discovery benchmark beside four methods on
the same three simulated systems: a **plain model**, the same language model
with the same task but no way to measure; **random selection**, settings drawn
at random and fitted by least squares; a **grid** of settings fitted by least
squares; and a grid fitted by **sparse identification**, the symbolic fit of
the discovery package. One judge scores them all on the same held-out
settings, and the build checks, for every row, whether the comparison with the
agent is one the protocol allows.

## Assumptions

1. **The systems and the judge are those of the benchmark.** The projectile,
   the spring, and the central force, each under its protocol: the same hidden
   value, held-out settings, seed, and tolerance for every method. A method
   recovers the law when its claim's held-out error is at most
   `{python} result["tolerance"]`, and a baseline only when its fit is also
   consistent with the noise.
2. **The agent is the partial condition.** On each system the agent's run is
   the run of the benchmark in which it was told the names of the parameters
   to report, but not the form of the law.
3. **The plain model gets the same task.** Its task text is the agent's; its
   system prompt says that it cannot measure, and its only tool is `submit`. It
   was recorded once on each system, like the agent.
4. **A budget is the number of probes allowed.** The agent and the baselines
   are each allowed `{python} result["budget"]` probes. The baselines spend
   all of them; the agent spends what it chooses. A method allowed a different
   number is a different comparison, and the build says so.
5. **The baselines are deterministic.** Each is a fixed procedure with a fixed
   seed, so it gives the same result on every build and can be rerun on any
   number of seeds at no cost.

## What each comparison measures {#explanation}

Each method differs from the agent in a known way, and the comparison measures
exactly that difference:

- **Plain model**: it has no probes, so the comparison measures what the
  experiments add to what the model knows.
- **Random selection**: the settings are not chosen, so it measures what
  choosing the experiments adds.
- **Grid with least squares**: the settings are fixed in advance, so it
  measures the same against a regular design.
- **Grid with sparse identification**: the form of the law is searched for,
  not given, so it measures what the model's knowledge of forms adds.

A comparison is **meaningful** when nothing else differs: the same system, the
same hidden world, the same held-out settings and tolerance, and the same
number of probes allowed. The build's check, `comparable`, reads these from
the protocols of the two entries:

```{python}
#| echo: false
from pbc.discovery.benchmark import comparable

excerpt(comparable)
```

The plain model fails one condition by design: it is allowed no probe. Its
comparison with the agent is still informative, but it measures the tools and
the probes together, and the check says the budgets differ rather than
calling it a like-for-like comparison.

held-out settings within the tolerance.]{.claim type="numerically-verified"
scope="one recorded run per system, the simulated systems of the benchmark"
evidence="ev3-entries replay-plainprojectile replay-plainoscillator

that value, so on these systems the tools are not optional.

evidence="ev3-entries ev3-tally"} The agent's failure is the spring, where its
readings supported a recovery (the benchmark lesson shows the fit) and its
estimate did not.

The last row is random selection with exactly the number of probes the agent
spent on each system. It recovers the law everywhere, and the check marks it
not comparable with the agent: it was allowed fewer probes. It answers a
different question, how well a method does with the agent's spending rather
than its allowance, and both questions are fair as long as they are not
confused.

## Limits {#limits}

- **One agent run per system.** The baselines can be run on any number of
  seeds; the agent was recorded once. A ranking of the agent against them needs
  many agent runs, and the exercise shows what the baselines look like over
  many seeds.
- **Easy systems favour simple baselines.** Each law has one or two parameters
  and a known form, which least squares exploits directly. A system whose form
  is unknown, or whose informative settings are rare, could reverse the order;
  this lesson does not test one.
- **Round hidden values flatter the agent.** On two systems the agent rounded
  onto the hidden value and scored zero, better than any fit. That is luck of
  the benchmark's design, not skill the score can show.
- **The symbolic fit has a fixed library.** Sparse identification finds only
  sums of its terms; on the spring it has none and makes no claim. A richer
  library, or the power-law search of the symbolic-regression lesson, would be
  a different baseline. The power-law search assumes noise proportional to the
  reading, which these systems do not have.
- **The plain model's system prompt differs from the agent's.** It has to,
  because the agent's says how many probes it has. The task text is the same.
- **The recordings are not API runs.** As in the benchmark lesson: Claude Code
  sessions, no token count or price reported.

::: {.exercise .self-check}
Random selection with least squares recovered the law on all three systems,
the agent on two. Which conclusion does this lesson support?

::: {.choices}
::: {.choice}
Random selection is a better discovery method than the agent.

::: {.feedback}
One agent run per system cannot rank the two, and the systems are easy for a
fit that is told the form of the law. The comparison is fair; the sample is
too small for a ranking.
:::
:::

::: {.choice correct="true"}
On these systems, with the same budget allowed, the baselines recovered every
law and the agent missed one; the plain model, which could not measure,
missed all three, so the measurements, not the model's prior, found the
hidden values.

::: {.feedback}
Right. Each part is a statement about these runs under one judge, and the
plain model is the control that shows what the tools add.
:::
:::

::: {.choice}
The agent used fewer probes, so it is more efficient than the baselines.

::: {.feedback}
The baselines spend their whole allowance by design. Random selection with the
agent's number of probes also recovered every law, so on these systems spending
fewer probes is not an advantage only the agent has.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.solution}
The supported conclusion is the narrow one: one judge, the same allowance,
these runs. The plain model shows that the hidden values come from the
experiments. Ranking the agent against the baselines needs many agent runs on
many hidden values.
:::
:::

## Exercises

::: {.exercise}
A baseline can be rerun at no cost. Run random selection with least squares
with the agent's number of probes on each system, over twenty seeds, and
count how often it recovers the law. What does this tell you about reading
one agent run?

::: {.solution}
```{python}
#| echo: false
excerpt(experiment.seeds)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
result.table("ev3-seeds")
```

With so few probes, random selection fails on some seeds of the spring: a
handful of random times may miss the late, informative ones, or fit an alias
of the frequency. One run of any method is one draw from a distribution like
this. The agent's single failure on the spring could be its usual result or a
bad draw; only many runs tell which.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
The plain model is allowed no probe, and the check marks its comparison with
the agent "not meaningful". Is the comparison then useless? Say what it
measures, and what a fairer control for the value of the model's knowledge
would be.

::: {.solution}
It is not useless: it measures what the tools and the probes together add to
the model's prior, which is the question "does tool use help?" in its plainest
form. It cannot separate the value of choosing experiments from the value of
having data. Two controls separate them: the baselines with the same
allowance, which have data but no model, and the matched random selection,
which has the agent's number of probes but no choice. The plain model is the
control for the opposite end: the model without data.
:::
:::
